scenes.title: A small piece of a company
scenes.caption: A stock represents ownership. One share is one unit of that ownership.

scenes.title: Cash becomes shares
scenes.caption: Buy 2 shares at $100 each: spend $200 in cash and own 2 shares.

scenes.title: Value can rise
scenes.caption: If each share reaches $110, 2 shares are worth $220. That is a $20 unrealized gain.

scenes.title: Value can fall
scenes.caption: If each share falls to $90, 2 shares are worth $180. That is a $20 unrealized loss.

scenes.title: Practice the idea
scenes.caption: Use virtual cash in Sprout. A real stock never guarantees a profit.

scenes.title: What is a day trade?
scenes.caption: Opening and closing a position during the same trading day.

scenes.title: A same-day example
scenes.caption: Buy at 10 a.m. Monday. Sell at 2 p.m. Monday. That is a day trade.

scenes.title: A different-day example
scenes.caption: Buy on Monday and sell on Friday. This is not a same-day trade.

scenes.title: Speed brings risk
scenes.caption: Fast price movements can create losses quickly. Frequent trades do not guarantee income.

scenes.title: Learn before you trade
scenes.caption: Sprout runs simulated prices 24/7. Real US regular sessions generally run 9:30 a.m.–4 p.m. Eastern on trading days.

scenes.title: Four prices. One candle.
scenes.caption: A candle summarizes the open, high, low, and close for one time period.

scenes.title: The body
scenes.caption: The body connects the opening and closing prices. It shows the net price change.

scenes.title: The wicks
scenes.caption: Thin lines extend to the highest and lowest prices reached during the period.

scenes.title: Green and red
scenes.caption: Green closes above the open. Red closes below the open. Neither color predicts the next candle.

scenes.title: Try the LIVE view
scenes.caption: Sprout LIVE candles cover 30 seconds each. Inspect a candle and compare its four prices.

scenes.title: Two ways to place an order
scenes.caption: A market order prioritizes execution. A limit order sets a price condition.

scenes.title: Market: trade now
scenes.caption: Sprout fills at its displayed simulated quote. Real market orders may fill at a different price.

scenes.title: Buy limit: at or below
scenes.caption: With a $100 buy limit, the purchase can fill at $100 or less. It cannot fill above $100.

scenes.title: A limit may never fill
scenes.caption: If the price stays above $100, that buy limit waits. A chosen price is not a guaranteed trade.

scenes.title: Practice both
scenes.caption: Sprout checks pending limits while the app is open. Real trading has spreads, slippage, and other costs.

title: Plan your risk and share size

scenes.title: Decide what you can lose
scenes.caption: A risk budget is the planned loss on one trade, not the cash spent buying shares.

scenes.title: Start with a simple example
scenes.caption: 1% of a $1,000 practice account is a $10 planned risk budget.

scenes.title: Measure the stop distance
scenes.caption: A $100 entry and $98 stop give a $2 planned loss per share.

scenes.title: Calculate the share count
scenes.caption: $10 risk budget divided by $2 per share gives 5 shares, costing $500 to buy.

scenes.title: Allow for uncertainty
scenes.caption: A real stop can fill worse than planned. Try these numbers in Sprout’s Tools tab.

scenes.title: Think areas, not promises
scenes.caption: Support is an area where buying previously slowed a fall. Resistance is where selling slowed a rise.

scenes.title: Notice repeated reactions
scenes.caption: If price repeatedly turns near $100 or $110, mark those areas to study.

scenes.title: A level can break
scenes.caption: A past reaction does not guarantee another. Price can move through either area.

scenes.title: Check the wider picture
scenes.caption: Compare the trend and timeframe. A chart pattern alone is not a reason to enter.

scenes.title: Practice a decision
scenes.caption: In the Chart lab, describe what you see and plan a possible loss before choosing an entry.

scenes.title: A fund holds investments
scenes.caption: An exchange-traded fund, or ETF, holds a collection of assets and trades on an exchange.

scenes.title: Spread concentration
scenes.caption: Holding different investments can reduce dependence on one company’s result.

scenes.title: Look inside the basket
scenes.caption: Two funds may own many of the same companies. More tickers do not always mean more variety.

scenes.title: Risk still remains
scenes.caption: A broad stock fund can fall with the market. Funds also have fees and different strategies.

scenes.title: Compare before choosing
scenes.caption: Study a fund’s holdings, costs, and purpose. Practice comparing stocks and ETFs in Sprout.

title: Research a company before a trade

scenes.title: Start with the business
scenes.caption: Explain what the company sells, who buys it, and how it earns money.

scenes.title: Check public sources
scenes.caption: Use company reports and SEC filings. Check dates instead of relying on a social media headline.

scenes.title: Study finances and risks
scenes.caption: Compare revenue, cash flow, debt, and business risks. One strong number is not the whole story.

scenes.title: Write what could change your mind
scenes.caption: State your idea, supporting evidence, and what would make the idea no longer fit.

scenes.title: Separate research from prediction
scenes.caption: Understanding a company does not guarantee a price move. Record your reasoning in a practice journal.

scenes.title: Notice the urge
scenes.caption: FOMO is fear of missing out. Revenge trading is trying to win back a loss through another rushed trade.

scenes.title: A fast move is not a plan
scenes.caption: Seeing a price jump can create urgency. Feeling late does not make an entry suitable.

scenes.title: A loss does not owe you a win
scenes.caption: Increasing size to recover money can make the next loss larger.

scenes.title: Pause before the next click
scenes.caption: Check your planned size, exit, and reason for trading. Passing on a trade is an available choice.

scenes.title: Track the feeling
scenes.caption: Use Sprout’s mood check-in and journal. Review your habits rather than judging yourself by one result.

scenes.title: Know what comes in
scenes.caption: Start with take-home income: the money available after deductions.

scenes.title: Give essentials a place
scenes.caption: List housing, food, bills, and debt payments. Include costs that arrive less often.

scenes.title: Leave room for goals
scenes.caption: Plan affordable saving and optional spending. Adjust the plan when income or expenses change.

scenes.title: Use a worked example
scenes.caption: $2,000 income minus $1,500 planned spending leaves $500 for savings and other goals.

scenes.title: Protect money you need
scenes.caption: Do not treat essential bill money as trading capital. You can start learning with virtual money today.

scenes.title: Growth can build on growth
scenes.caption: Compounding means interest or returns can apply to earlier interest or returns as well as the starting amount.

scenes.title: A simple first year
scenes.caption: At a hypothetical 5% yearly rate, $1,000 becomes $1,050 after one year.

scenes.title: The next year builds on $1,050
scenes.caption: At the same hypothetical rate, another $52.50 brings the balance to $1,102.50.

scenes.title: It can work against you
scenes.caption: Debt interest can also compound. Rates, fees, payments, and terms affect the result.

scenes.title: Examples are not forecasts
scenes.caption: Investment returns vary and may be negative. Compare assumptions before using any growth projection.

scenes.title: Compare with what you paid
scenes.caption: A price change creates a gain or loss relative to your purchase price.

scenes.title: Count every share
scenes.caption: Buy 2 shares at $100 and sell at $110: a $20 gain before costs.

scenes.title: Use percentages to compare
scenes.caption: $10 gained on a $100 share is a 10% return. Percentages put different-sized trades in context.

scenes.title: Realized versus unrealized
scenes.caption: A result on shares you still hold is unrealized. Selling makes that result realized.

scenes.title: Include the whole picture
scenes.caption: Fees and slippage affect real results. Sprout’s Profit / loss explorer lets you try hypothetical exits.
